name: Kaya 0.1.86
changelog: Board markup in reviews. Kaya now draws the annotations a teaching record carries — triangles, squares, circles, crosses and letter/number labels — on the board as you step through a game.

history.1: First build: offline board, full rules and scoring, SGF, and a computer opponent.
history.2: Dark theme (Crake palette) with a light/dark toggle, plus a tidier header.
history.3: Crake electric-teal palette, stone-click sound, and a richer board.
history.5: Faster, stronger bot and a purpose-built tablet (landscape) layout.
history.6: Fail-safe update install (browser fallback) and a richer wood texture.
history.7: NFC tap-to-share (tap another phone to open Kaya's download page).
history.8: Stronger bot: RAVE search shares each playout across related moves for more purposeful, tougher play at the same speed.
history.9: Tighter bot: prunes pointless self-atari moves before searching, so it never slams a stone into nothing and reads deeper.
history.10: The computer ends decided games gracefully: when you pass and it is settled and ahead, it passes back instead of playing on.
history.11: A more handsome board: a proper goban frame with a heavier outer border and hairline inner lines, scaled to the board size.
history.12: A more tactical opponent: it now values captures, threats, and rescues by group size, so it goes after whole groups and defends its big ones.
history.13: The About screen now shows the real installed version, so every update is visible on the phone.
history.14: A far more tactical opponent: it now blocks when you atari it, and it puts your stones in atari and captures. Forcing moves no longer fade out of its reading.
history.15: Better shape: the bot now connects its own stones into strong groups and wedges to cut yours apart, so its stones work together.
history.16: The opponent now reads ladders: it favours ataris that actually run a stone down and capture, and no longer treats escaping ataris as wins.
history.17: A ko marker: when a recapture is forbidden by the ko rule, the board shows a small square on that point so it is clear why and where you cannot play yet.
history.18: A stronger read at the same speed: the bot's playouts are now forcing (they press weak groups into atari and follow up), so it judges fights far more accurately.
history.19: A clearer result: when the game is scored, each side shows where its points came from (territory + captures, or stones + area) with komi.
history.20: Easier to follow: the status line now names the move just played (e.g. "White played G5"), so you can find your opponent's stone at a glance.
history.21: Kaya remembers your setup: the New Game dialog opens on the size, ruleset, handicap, opponent, and difficulty you last played.
history.22: Resign now asks first (one tap arms it, the button becomes Confirm resign), so a stray tap can't end your game. New Game also truly remembers your last setup across launches.
history.23: Sensible openings: the computer now starts in the corners like real games, instead of dropping its first stones anywhere along the side.
history.24: No more hopeless ladders: the bot now reads whether a caught group can escape and stops running one that is lost, instead of feeding you more stones.
history.25: A tougher default: the Medium computer (where every new game starts) now reads deeper and plays stronger, while still moving in about a second.
history.26: Better opening shape: in the opening the computer no longer attaches onto your lone stones, it approaches from a distance and takes big points instead.
history.27: Games feel fresh: the computer now varies its play from game to game instead of opening the same corner and answering identically every time.
history.28: Complete saved games: SGF exports now record the ruleset and the result on a resignation, so they open with the right rules and winner in other Go software.
history.29: Sharper fighting: the computer now spots a double atari (one move forking two of your groups) and no longer over-values touching a single group from several sides.
history.30: A smarter Easy opponent: it now saves its own groups when you atari them instead of letting them die, and varies its play from game to game.
history.31: Defends earlier: the computer reinforces a group that is down to two liberties and under attack, before you can push it into atari.
history.32: Opens more game files: SGFs with variations (game reviews, problem sets) now load along the main line instead of muddling every branch together.
history.33: Complete results in saved games: a game that ends by counting now records its final score in the SGF (e.g. B+12.5), not just resignations.
history.34: Graceful concessions: when the computer is hopelessly behind in a developed game it resigns instead of making you capture everything, but never early off a shaky read.
history.35: Share your games: on Android, Save SGF now opens the share sheet to send a finished game (with ruleset and result) to Files, Drive, email, or a chat.
history.36: A slightly sharper read: the computer no longer wastes exploration on pointless first-line moves, so its sense of who is ahead is cleaner and its play a touch stronger.
history.37: A more beautiful board: the wood now catches a soft warm light toward the centre and settles into richer edges, like a real lit goban. Lovely in the dark theme.
history.38: Glossier stones: each stone now catches a small point of light, so black slate and white shell look polished and three-dimensional against the lit board.
history.39: A more refined New Game dialog: settings sit under small-cap section headers with more breathing room, and a soft divider sets your choices apart from Start game. Tidy in both themes.
history.40: A polished Kaya mark: the two stones in the logo (and the little header mark) now catch the same shading and glossy light as the stones on the board, and the About logo lifts off the panel with a soft shadow.
history.41: Nicer player cards: the little Black and White stones on the two player pills are now real, shaded stones with a soft shadow, matching the board and logo. The White marker no longer fades into the cream panel.
history.42: A board with real depth: the wood now has a beveled edge, catching light along the top and left and settling into shadow at the bottom and right, so it reads as a solid slab of kaya on the table. Especially lovely in the dark theme.
history.43: Tidier scoring: when the game is counted, the territory marks are now smaller, softly rounded, and gently outlined, so they read as delicate points on the wood instead of heavy blocks. The white marks no longer melt into the board.
history.44: A nicer read-out: after a Hint, the who-is-ahead bar is now a glossy capsule with a soft sheen and a clean divider at the split, instead of a flat black and white block. The hint marker still points the way in the accent colour.
history.45: Buttons with a little life: Pass, Undo, Hint, New game and Resign now sit on a soft shadow like raised keys, catching a touch of light on top and sinking as you tap. A disabled button stays flat and quiet. Matches the depth of the board and stones.
history.46: One consistent look: the Menu button up top is now a raised key like the ones along the bottom, and its dropdown opens as clean, easy-to-tap rows. The whole app now feels cut from the same cloth.
history.47: A typeface with character: the Kaya name, the dialog titles and the game result now wear an elegant serif (Spectral), while the rest stays crisp and clean. A calm, timeless feel that suits an old game. Lovely in both themes.
history.48: The whole app now reads in a proper typeface: the body text moves to Fira Sans, a warm, clear humanist sans that pairs with the Spectral serif on the titles. Buttons, labels and the board coordinates all look crisper and more intentional, in both themes.
history.49: The players get their names in the good typeface too: Black and White on the two cards are now set in the Spectral serif, matching the Kaya wordmark and dialog titles, while the capture count and turn stay in the clean sans.
history.50: A little colophon: the About screen now credits the two typefaces that dress the app, and sets each name in its own face, Spectral in Spectral and Fira Sans in Fira Sans. A small mark of care, and a nod to the open-font makers.
history.51: A cleaner Menu: the dropdown now reads as a proper menu, clean full-width rows with a light touch of colour on the one you're pointing at and a soft divider between the file actions and the settings, instead of a stack of little outlined boxes.
history.52: A more tactile placement: when a stone lands it now grows in from a touch smaller and settles with a gentle overshoot, so playing a move feels a little more like setting a stone on the board. Subtle, in keeping with Kaya's calm.
history.53: Find the last move at a glance: the row and column of the last stone played are now picked out in colour along the board's edge, so the coordinates quietly point to where it landed, alongside the ring on the stone itself.
history.54: Captures that look the part: when stones are taken, they now lift off the board as the same polished stones, swelling a touch and fading away, instead of flattening into plain discs. A small, satisfying moment done properly.
history.55: A proper app icon: Kaya's launcher icon now wears the same look as the board, two glossy, sphere-shaded stones catching the light on warm lit wood, instead of flat shapes on a flat colour. The face of the app finally matches the app.
history.56: Friendlier setup: Handicap and Komi in the New Game dialog are now simple plus/minus steppers that match the rest of the buttons, instead of fiddly drag-to-change number fields. Easier to nudge with a thumb, and it looks the part.
history.57: A gentler count: when a game is scored, the territory marks now fade and settle into place over a moment, so the board resolves into its territories instead of snapping to the result. A calm little payoff at the end of a game.
history.58: Kaya's read settles in: after a Hint, the who-is-ahead bar now sweeps from even to the estimate, with the percentages counting up as it lands, so the verdict arrives with a considered little motion instead of snapping into place.
history.59: Real shell stones: the white stones now carry the faintest clamshell grain, the fine growth lines a real yuki Go stone shows, so they read as polished shell rather than plain white. Barely there, but it is the sort of detail a Go player notices.
history.60: The hint arrives gracefully: when you ask for a Hint, the suggested-move marker now eases onto the board as the read settles, so Kaya's whole suggestion appears with one calm motion rather than snapping in.
history.61: One last stock control gone: the 'check for updates automatically' setting in About is now a proper pill toggle that slides and turns the accent colour, matching every other control in the app, instead of a plain tick box.
history.62: Better on a tablet: in the wide landscape layout the two player cards now stack down the side panel, each getting its own roomy card, instead of being squeezed side by side. The upright phone layout is unchanged.
history.63: A tidier dialog: opening New Game or About now dims the whole screen behind it, including the side panel in the wide tablet layout, instead of leaving the side controls lit up. The dim is even everywhere now.
history.64: A small fix to the count: the score readout now says '1 capture' rather than '1 captures' (and likewise for a single stone in Chinese scoring), so the result reads properly when the number is one.
history.65: A living wait: while the computer is thinking its move, the status line now shows a gently animated 'Kaya is thinking…' with the dots cycling, so on a slower search it's clearly working rather than frozen.
history.66: Steadier controls: arming Resign now shows a compact 'Confirm' on the button (with the status line spelling out what it does), so the row of controls no longer bumps a button onto a second line while you decide.
history.67: The move you just played stands out: in the status line, the coordinate of the last move is now picked out in the accent colour (matching the highlight along the board's edge), so 'White played D5' points you right to it. Also tidied a stray double space.
history.68: The last-move ring now looks right on every board size. Its outline used to be a fixed thickness, which read a touch chunky on the small stones of a 19x19 board; it now scales with the stone, staying elegant on 9x9 and proportionally lighter on 19x19.
history.69: Dialogs read as crisp floating cards in the dark theme. The New Game and About panels lean on a drop shadow to lift off the background, but a shadow is invisible against the dark theme's near-black, so the panel used to blur into it. They now carry a fine outline that defines the edge in both themes.
history.70: The dead-stone mark now belongs to the board. When you mark stones dead during scoring, the small × over each was a lone bright red — the only pure red in the app. It is now a warm terracotta that sits in Kaya's palette, while staying just as clear on both pale and dark stones.
history.71: Tap-to-share now opens the playable Kaya. Tapping your phone to another (NFC) used to send them to the download page; it now opens the live, playable Kaya board in their browser — ready to play.
history.72: Review your games. A new bar below the board steps you back through every move — Start, Back, Next, End — with each move named as you go, so you can see how the game unfolded. The board pauses while you study it and picks up right where you left off when you tap End.
history.73: Explained hints. When you ask for a Hint, Kaya now tells you why it likes the move — whether it captures, puts a group in atari, saves one of yours, links your stones, cuts the opponent, or takes a big point — right alongside its read of who is ahead.
history.74: Move numbers in review. When you step back through a game, each stone now shows the move it was played on, so the whole order of play reads straight off the board.
history.75: Analyse your moves. While reviewing a game, tap Analyse and Kaya reads the position — who is ahead, and how much the move that reached it cost — so you can find exactly where a game turned.
history.76: Find your mistakes in one tap. A new Find mistakes button reviews a whole game at once and lists the moves that cost the most, so you can jump straight to your biggest swings instead of stepping through by hand.
history.77: Kaya shows a better move. While analysing a game in review, Kaya now marks the move it would play in each position and names it in the read, so you see not just where you went wrong but what to do instead.
history.78: A more composed tablet layout. In landscape on a tablet, the side panel now sits the player cards at the top and the controls at the bottom, so it reads as a balanced column instead of everything crammed at the top.
history.79: Balanced player cards and a considered portrait layout on tablets. The two player cards now always match in width (the inactive one no longer shrinks to a stub beside the active one), which also tidies the portrait tablet view so it reads as a real tablet layout rather than a stretched phone.
history.80: A quiet tablet touch. On a tablet, the card of whoever is to move now breathes a soft, slow glow in the accent colour — barely there, never flashing. A small sign the tablet layout was made with care.
history.81: The mark comes to life on tablets. On a tablet, the two-stone Kaya mark in the top-left now takes a slow, graceful turn once every 30 seconds and settles back — a small, living detail, and only on tablets.
history.82: A crisp opening. Instead of snapping in, Kaya now fades up gently from the background as it opens, with the board settling to full size — a small, premium entrance on every device.
history.83: A tougher opponent, if you want one. New Game now offers a fourth level, Strong, that reads about three times as deep as Hard. It takes several seconds a move but plays a distinctly harder game.
history.84: Open games in Kaya. You can now share an SGF to Kaya, or open an .sgf file with it, and the game loads ready to review — so the whole review, Find mistakes, and suggested-move suite works on real games, not just ones played in Kaya.
history.85: Loaded games show their record. When you open an SGF, the player cards now wear the real names and ranks, and a header shows the event, date, and result in plain words — so a loaded game reads like the record it is, not just stones on a board.
history.86: Read the commentary. When you open a commented game or teaching record, Kaya now shows each move's comment in a soft card as you step through it — so studying an annotated game reads the way it should.
history.87: Board markup in reviews. Kaya now draws the annotations a teaching record carries — triangles, squares, circles, crosses and letter/number labels — on the board as you step through a game.
